worksheet.title: Find the Loop Bug
worksheet.subtitle: Ontario Math C3.2 — read, find, and fix code
worksheet.learning_goal: I can find the bug in a loop and fix it.

parts.title: Coders fix bugs
text: A bug is a mistake in code. Coders read carefully to FIND the bug, then FIX it — like finding a wrong step in a set of directions.
A loop bug is usually one of two things: the wrong repeat number, or a wrong block inside. Help Bit find and fix them.

parts.title: Bit should JUMP 5 times — but this loop is buggy
parts.note: Bit only jumps 3 times. The repeat number is wrong — it should be 5.

parts.caption: Find the wrong number, then fix it: repeat 3 → repeat 5.

parts.title: Find the bug
parts.prompt: Bit should jump 5 times, but the loop says repeat 3. What is wrong? What should the repeat number be? ______

parts.title: Fix the inside
parts.prompt: Bit should stamp red, blue. But the loop's inside is: stamp red, stamp red. Which block is wrong, and what should it be?

parts.title: Fix the count
parts.prompt: Bit should move 30 steps in total, 10 each time. The loop says repeat 2. What repeat number fixes it? ______

parts.title: Challenge
parts.prompt: This loop is repeat 4 with TWO "move" blocks inside. Bit moved 8 times but should move only 4. Is the bug the repeat number or the inside blocks? Fix it and explain.

parts.title: Big idea
parts.text: To debug a loop, first say what it SHOULD do, then read what it DOES. The bug is usually the repeat number or a block inside — change the one that is wrong.

parts.title: Goal
parts.text: Students read a buggy loop, decide whether the bug is the repeat count or an inside block, and fix it so the code matches the goal (Ontario C3.2).

parts.title: Curriculum (Ontario Math 2020, Strand C3)
text: C3.1 — solve problems and create computational representations of mathematical situations by writing and executing code, including code that involves sequential, concurrent, and repeating events.
C3.2 — read and alter existing code, including code that involves sequential, concurrent, and repeating events, and describe how changes to the code affect the outcomes.

parts.title: Materials
parts.text: A block-coding app (Scratch-style) to project — show a buggy loop and fix it live; the printed worksheet + a pencil per student.

parts.title: Run it (about 30 min)
text: 1. Hook: read directions with a wrong step — finding the mistake is debugging.
2. Project the buggy repeat-3 (should be 5) loop; find and fix it together.
3. Students do Exercises 1–4 (Ex 4 is the stretch), solo or in pairs.
4. Share answers; land the big idea: say what it SHOULD do, then find the wrong part.

parts.title: Answer key (checked by the run-gate)
text: Ex 1 — the repeat number is wrong; it should be repeat 5.
Ex 2 — the second block is wrong; change "stamp red" to "stamp blue".
Ex 4 (challenge) — the inside is the bug: two move blocks; remove one (repeat 4 × 1 = 4 moves).

parts.title: Watch for & differentiate
text: Common slip: changing the repeat number in Ex 4 when the bug is the extra inside block.
Support: write the GOAL number first, then compare to what the code does.
Extend: a different Ex 4 fix — repeat 2 with two moves also gives 4.

parts.title: Success looks like
parts.text: The student says what the code should do, finds whether the bug is the count or an inside block, and fixes it to match the goal (Ex 1–4).
